slides.title: Slingshot Secrets
slides.kicker: How a gulel stores and gives energy
bullets: Pull back a slingshot (gulel) and release it: the stretched elastic band shoots the object forward.
An archer pulls the string of a bow, bending its arms; when released, the bow springs back and the arrow flies off.
In both cases the stretched band or bent bow applies a force on the object in contact, setting it in motion and giving it kinetic energy.
slides.note: Gulel ki yaad hai? Stretch first, speed later!

slides.title: Work Gets Stored
slides.kicker: Deforming an object is like charging it
bullets: The coins, ball and arrow gain kinetic energy they did not originally possess; the energy must come from the stretched band or bent bow.
A deformed object has the capacity to do work because of its shape; the work done to cause the deformation gets stored in it.
Stretch or compress a spring and you do work on it; the spring stores this energy while it is held in the deformed state.

items: Energy is stored in its shape

slides.note: Stored energy sits quietly inside the shape.

slides.title: Springs Push Back
bullets: You need an external force to overcome the internal forces inside a spring and deform it.
Once you remove the external force, the internal forces undo the deformation, and in the process the spring can carry out work.
This is how internal forces allow energy to be stored in a deformed object.
slides.note: Andar ki taakat hi kaam karti hai!

slides.title: Stored by Arrangement
bullets: Energy can be stored not only by deforming an object but also by changing the arrangement of objects in a system.
Like poles of magnets repel each other, while unlike poles attract each other.
Separating the unlike poles of two magnets requires applying a force, and that work gets stored in the new arrangement.
slides.note: Same idea, new trick: rearrange instead of deform.

slides.title: Meet Mechanical Energy
bullets: The sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy of an object is called its mechanical energy.
A moving, falling object usually carries both kinds of energy at the same time.
Let us track both energies for an object of mass m lifted to a height h and then dropped.
slides.note: KE plus PE: motion plus position in one number.

slides.title: Top vs Mid-Fall
slides.kicker: mgh holds steady all the way down
bullets: At point A, height h, dropped from rest: potential energy is mgh, kinetic energy is 0, so mechanical energy is mgh.
After falling for a time t to point B, the velocity has grown and the height has shrunk.
At B the lost potential energy exactly equals the gained kinetic energy, so the mechanical energy is still mgh.

right.title: While falling at B
items: kinetic energy = the loss made up

slides.note: PE girti hai, KE badhti hai, total set rehta hai.

slides.title: Conservation Stated
bullets: As the object falls, its potential energy decreases while its kinetic energy increases.
The lost potential energy is converted into kinetic energy during the motion.
If no other external forces act, an object moving under gravity keeps its mechanical energy: conservation of mechanical energy.

items: Object falls: PE turns into KE

slides.note: Upar se girte hue, energy ka hisaab nahi badalta.

slides.title: Pendulum Check
slides.kicker: The bob keeps its energy book
bullets: Activity 7.2: set up a simple pendulum and draw a horizontal line above the position of the hanging bob.
Take the bob to point P at the level of the line and let it go.
The bob climbs to nearly the same level on the other side: potential energy at the ends, kinetic energy at the bottom.

slides.title: Same Work, Different Rush
bullets: Carry your bag up a flight of stairs to your classroom and notice how it feels.
Running up in one minute feels very different from walking up slowly in five minutes.
The same work is done in both cases; the difference between them is described by a quantity called power.
slides.note: Same kaam, alag speed: yahi power hai.

slides.title: Defining Power
slides.kicker: Work done divided by time taken
bullets: Power is defined as the rate at which work is done.
The average power P is the work done W divided by the time taken t: P = W/t.
To do more work in the same time needs more power; to do the same work in a shorter time also needs more power.

slides.title: Watts and Horsepower
bullets: The SI unit of power is the watt (W): 1 watt is 1 joule of work done per second, so 1 W = 1 J/s.
Car engines and pumps used to lift water are often measured in horsepower (hp); 1 hp = 746 W.
The unit watt is named in honour of James Watt, known for steam engines that could produce motion and move wheels.
slides.note: James Watt ke naam par watt.

slides.title: Why Simple Machines
bullets: Everyday life often asks us to do work against gravity or other forces, such as lifting or moving heavy objects.
The total work required for a task cannot be reduced, but the task can be made easier.
Devices that change the magnitude or direction of the force to be applied are called simple machines.

slides.title: Effort, Load, Advantage
slides.kicker: Three words to judge a machine
bullets: The force we apply to a machine is called the effort.
The force that needs to be overcome is called the load.
Mechanical advantage is the ratio of the load to the effort; it describes how a machine changes the magnitude of the applied force.

slides.title: What Machines Cannot Do
bullets: A simple machine can reduce the force you need or turn it in a friendlier direction.
It cannot reduce the total work required for the task.
Whatever you save in force, you pay back by pushing over a larger distance or in a new direction.
slides.note: Machine force badalti hai, kaam nahi.

slides.title: The Flagpole Pulley
slides.kicker: Pull down, the flag goes up
bullets: You may have seen a flag or a load being raised while the rope is pulled downward; a pulley fixed at the top does this.
A pulley is a wheel with a groove that guides a rope.
It is easier for us to pull downward than to lift a load by applying an upward force directly.

slides.title: Fixed Pulley, Direction Hero
bullets: A fixed pulley does not reduce the magnitude of the force required; it only changes its direction.
Since the effort and the load are equal in magnitude, the mechanical advantage of a fixed pulley is 1.
Its gift is convenience: you pull down comfortably while the load moves up.

left.title: Lifting directly
items: upward force equal to the load

slides.title: Movable Pulley Systems
slides.kicker: Team up pulleys for big loads
bullets: Movable pulleys or a system of pulleys can have a mechanical advantage greater than 1.
They can lift much heavier objects with much smaller effort; in a movable pulley system the load is attached to the movable pulley.
One end of the rope is fixed to a point while the other end is free to apply effort; elevators and cranes use pulleys widely.

items: Rope end fixed to a support

slides.title: The Too-Heavy Box
bullets: To lift a heavy box onto a platform, lifting it vertically requires an upward force equal to its weight.
What if the box is too heavy for you to lift directly?
You can place the box on a smooth inclined plank and push it up the plank to the platform instead.
slides.note: Seedha uthana mushkil? Raste mein dhyaan do.

slides.title: Ramp Experiment
bullets: Activity 7.3: pull a cart attached to a spring balance up a plank about 1.5 m long, reaching a stool or book pile about 0.5 m high.
Lifted vertically and steadily, the balance reads the force equal to the weight of the cart.
Pulled along the plank, the reading is smaller: the ramp asks for less force.

items: Lift the cart vertically: reading = weight

slides.title: Gentler Slope, Longer Push
bullets: Reduce the angle of the plank and the force needed to pull the cart up to the same height decreases further.
The catch: you must apply the force over a larger distance to bring the cart to the same height.
The work done, the product of force and distance, is the same; a longer ramp asks for an even smaller force.

slides.title: Ramp Arithmetic
bullets: For a load of mass m, the load to overcome is the weight mg; the effort F pushes it up the length L to a height h.
Since the work done is the same on both paths: F times L equals mg times h, so F = mgh/L.
Mechanical advantage = load/effort = mg / (mgh/L) = L/h; a longer ramp gives a bigger advantage.

items: F x L = mg x h

slides.title: Erasers Lift a Stapler
slides.kicker: A scale and pencil do the trick
bullets: Activity 7.4: place a 30 cm scale over a pencil kept closer to one end of the scale.
Put the stapler on the end nearer the pencil and erasers on the other end.
A much heavier object like the stapler gets lifted by a much lighter eraser; the scale is working as a lever.

slides.title: Parts of a Lever
slides.kicker: Fulcrum, load, effort in one bar
bullets: A lever is a rigid bar, such as your scale, that can rotate about a fixed point, such as the point of contact with the pencil.
Its three main parts: fulcrum, the fixed point of rotation; load, the force to overcome; effort, the force applied.
The distance of the load from the fulcrum is the load arm; the distance of the effort from the fulcrum is the effort arm.

slides.title: Trade Distance for Force
slides.kicker: One end travels, the other presses
bullets: The end with the small effort F1 moves the larger distance d1; the other end applies a larger force F2 over a smaller distance d2.
The work done on one end of the lever is transferred to the other end: F1 d1 = F2 d2.
Thus, by increasing the effort arm, the lever applies a larger force to the load compared to the effort you put in.

slides.title: Beam Balance Lever
slides.kicker: Coins, cups and a level beam
bullets: A beam balance is an example of a lever; build one with a long scale, a string and two paper cups.
Tie the string tightly around the midpoint of the scale to act as the fulcrum, and hang the beam so it swings freely.
Fix the cups as pans at both ends, place identical coins as weights, and adjust until the beam is levelled.
A lever reduces the force needed to perform a task, but not the work itself.

items: Cups as pans at both ends

flashcards.front: What is potential energy?
flashcards.back: Energy stored in an object because of its changed shape or changed arrangement; it is a capacity to do work.

flashcards.front: In a slingshot, where does the ball's kinetic energy come from?
flashcards.back: From the work stored in the stretched elastic band; on release the band applies a force and gives the ball motion.

flashcards.front: Why can a released compressed spring do work?
flashcards.back: Its internal forces undo the deformation once the external force is removed, and it transfers stored energy to the object in contact.

flashcards.front: Name two ways energy can be stored in a system.
flashcards.back: By deforming an object like a spring, and by changing the arrangement of objects, like separating the unlike poles of magnets.

flashcards.front: What is mechanical energy?
flashcards.back: The sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy of an object.

flashcards.front: Mass m dropped from rest at height h: mechanical energy at the top?
flashcards.back: mgh, because the potential energy is mgh and the kinetic energy is 0 at the moment of release.

flashcards.front: What happens to PE and KE as an object falls freely?
flashcards.back: Potential energy decreases, kinetic energy increases by the same amount, and mechanical energy stays constant at mgh.

flashcards.front: State the conservation of mechanical energy.
flashcards.back: As an object moves due to the gravitational force, its mechanical energy remains the same if no other external forces act on it.

flashcards.front: In a pendulum swing, where is kinetic energy greatest?
flashcards.back: At the lowest point of the swing, where the bob moves fastest; at the extreme points the energy is potential.

flashcards.front: Define power.
flashcards.back: Power is the rate at which work is done: average power P equals the work done W divided by the time taken t.

flashcards.front: What is the SI unit of power and how is it defined?
flashcards.back: The watt (W); 1 watt equals 1 joule of work done per second, so 1 W = 1 J/s.

flashcards.front: One horsepower equals how many watts?
flashcards.back: 1 horsepower (hp) = 746 W; hp is used for car engines and pumps used to lift water.

flashcards.front: A weightlifter lifts 75 kg by 2 m in 5 s. What power does she need?
After which scientist is the unit of power named?
flashcards.back: James Watt, known for steam engines that could produce motion and move wheels.

flashcards.front: What is a simple machine?
flashcards.back: A device that changes the magnitude or direction of the force you apply, making a task easier without reducing the total work.

flashcards.front: Distinguish effort and load in a machine.
flashcards.back: Effort is the force we apply to the machine; load is the force that needs to be overcome.

flashcards.front: Write the formula for mechanical advantage.
flashcards.back: Mechanical advantage = load / effort, the ratio of the load to the effort.

flashcards.front: What is a pulley?
flashcards.back: A wheel with a groove that guides a rope, used to raise loads such as a flag.

flashcards.front: What does a fixed pulley change about your force?
flashcards.back: Only its direction, not its magnitude; the effort and load are equal, so its mechanical advantage is 1.

flashcards.front: How is the rope arranged in a movable pulley system?
flashcards.back: The load is attached to the movable pulley; one end of the rope is fixed to a point and the other end is free to apply effort.

flashcards.front: Where do you meet pulleys in daily life?
flashcards.back: In elevators and cranes, which use pulleys widely for the convenience they provide.

flashcards.front: What is an inclined plane?
flashcards.back: A simple machine that helps move a heavy load to a higher or lower level, like a smooth plank used as a ramp.

flashcards.front: What is the trade-off when you use a gentler ramp?
flashcards.back: The force needed becomes smaller, but you apply it over a larger distance; the work done stays the same.

flashcards.front: Mechanical advantage of an inclined plane of length L and height h?
flashcards.back: L/h. Since F x L = mg x h, the effort is mgh/L, so load/effort = L/h; a longer ramp gives a bigger advantage.

flashcards.front: What is a lever?
flashcards.back: A rigid bar that can rotate about a fixed point, used to lift heavy objects with a small force.

flashcards.front: Name the three main parts of a lever.
flashcards.back: The fulcrum, the fixed point about which it rotates; the load, the force to be overcome; and the effort, the force applied.

flashcards.front: Which distances are the load arm and the effort arm?
flashcards.back: Load arm: distance of the load from the fulcrum. Effort arm: distance of the effort from the fulcrum.

flashcards.front: How is work transferred between the two ends of a lever?
flashcards.back: The small effort times its larger distance equals the larger load force times its smaller distance: F1 d1 = F2 d2.

flashcards.front: Which everyday device is an example of a lever?
flashcards.back: A beam balance; its beam swings about the string tied at its midpoint, which acts as the fulcrum.

quiz.why: While held deformed, the energy of the spring is due to its configuration or shape.

quiz.q: Separating the unlike poles of two magnets requires you to...

converted fully into kinetic energy at once

quiz.q: Doing the same work in half the time requires power that is...

quiz.q: An inclined plane is a simple machine that helps move a heavy load to a...

quiz.why: The fulcrum is the fixed point about which the lever rotates.

quiz.q: A beam balance is an example of a...

examples.title: Jet Lands on an Aircraft Carrier
examples.problem: A jet aircraft of mass 15000 kg lands on the deck of an aircraft carrier. A hook on its tail is caught by a wire stretched across the deck; the wire exerts an approximately constant backward force of 367500 N and stops the jet within 100 m. What was the velocity of the aircraft just before the wire caught the hook?
steps: The change in kinetic energy equals the work done by the wire: initial KE = (1/2) x 15000 x v^2, and the final KE = 0 J.
The displacement of the aircraft and the force of the wire are in opposite directions, so the work done by the wire is negative.
Work done by the wire = F x s = 367500 N x (-100 m) = -36750000 J, which must equal 0 - (1/2) x 15000 x v^2.
Convert: 70 m/s x 3600 s / 1000 m = 252 km/h.
examples.answer: 70 m/s, that is 252 km/h, directed towards the aircraft carrier.

examples.title: Weightlifter's Power
examples.problem: A weightlifter lifts a 75 kg mass by 2 m in 5 seconds. How much power does she require for this task?
steps: The work done equals mgh = 75 kg x 10 m/s^2 x 2 m.
Power = work done / time taken = 1500 J / 5 s.

examples.title: Engine Powers a Car
examples.problem: A car of mass 1000 kg starts from rest and reaches a speed of 72 km/h in 10 seconds. Calculate the power of the engine required to achieve this start.
steps: Convert the final velocity: 72 km/h = 72000 m per 3600 s = 20 m/s; the initial velocity u = 0 m/s.
Work done by the engine in 10 s = final kinetic energy minus initial kinetic energy = (1/2) x 1000 kg x (20 m/s)^2 - 0 J = 200000 J.
Power = work done / time = 200000 J / 10 s.

examples.title: Ramp Rescue
examples.problem: A box of weight 600 N must be raised onto a platform 1 m high. Instead of lifting it straight up, you push it up a smooth plank 5 m long, as in Activity 7.3. Find the effort needed and the mechanical advantage of the ramp.
steps: The load is the weight 600 N; the ramp has length L = 5 m and height h = 1 m.
The work done is the same on both paths: effort x L = load x h, so effort = (600 x 1) / 5 = 120 N.
Mechanical advantage = load / effort = 600 / 120 = 5, which equals L/h = 5/1.
Check the work: 120 N x 5 m = 600 J, the same as lifting 600 N through 1 m.
examples.answer: Effort = 120 N and mechanical advantage = 5; the ramp trades distance for force while the work stays 600 J.

steps.label: Store by shape
steps.detail: Stretching a band, bending a bow or compressing a spring stores the work you did on it.

steps.label: Store by arrangement
steps.detail: Separating the unlike poles of magnets also stores energy by changing the arrangement of a system.

steps.label: Release and move
steps.detail: The deformed object returns to its original shape and hands its stored energy to the object in contact as kinetic energy.

steps.label: Conserve mechanical energy
steps.detail: In free fall, lost potential energy becomes kinetic energy, so KE plus PE stays mgh.

steps.label: Watch the pendulum
steps.detail: The bob trades potential and kinetic energy every swing and returns to nearly the same height.

steps.label: Rate it with power
steps.detail: Power equals work divided by time, measured in watts; 1 horsepower is 746 W.

steps.label: Change force or direction
steps.detail: Simple machines ease a task by changing the force, without reducing the total work.

steps.label: Pull with pulleys
steps.detail: A fixed pulley reverses your pull with mechanical advantage 1; pulley systems can do better than 1.

steps.label: Push up ramps
steps.detail: An inclined plane lowers the force by stretching the push over a longer distance; MA = L/h.

steps.label: Press on levers
steps.detail: A long effort arm turns a small push into a large load force, with F1 d1 = F2 d2.
